hook: Mrs. Okafor, 71, suddenly becomes short of breath two days after chest pain. Her doctor hears a new whooshing sound with every beat. An ultrasound shows why: one of the small muscles that holds the cords of her mitral valve has torn, and the valve now flips backward into the left atrium each time the left ventricle squeezes.

prereq.q: Which layer of the heart wall lines the inside of the heart and covers its valves?
prereq.why: The endocardium is the endothelial lining of every space inside the heart, and it covers the valve cusps. The epicardium covers the outside, and the myocardium is the muscle in between.

prereq.q: By definition, which way does an artery carry blood?
prereq.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it toward the heart. Capillaries are the tiny vessels between them.

prereq.q: Blood flows through a tube from region A to region B. What must be true?
options: Pressure is higher at B than at A
Pressure is higher at A than at B
Pressure is equal at A and B
prereq.why: Fluid flows down a pressure gradient, from higher pressure to lower pressure. With no pressure difference, there is no flow.

anatomy.caption: The heart opened in a frontal plane. Hide the labels and name each chamber, septum, valve and great vessel.

chain.cause: The ventricle muscle contracts, raising the pressure of the blood inside the ventricle.
chain.effect: Blood pushes up on the cusps of the atrioventricular valve, and the cusps meet and seal the opening.

chain.cause: The papillary muscles, part of the same ventricle wall, contract along with it.
chain.effect: They pull the chordae tendineae tight.

chain.cause: The taut chordae tendineae hold the cusp edges down.
chain.effect: The cusps cannot flip up into the atrium, so blood does not flow backward into the atrium.

chain.cause: With the atrioventricular valve sealed, ventricular pressure keeps rising until it is higher than the pressure in the artery.
chain.effect: Blood presses the semilunar valve's cusps flat against the artery wall and flows out into the artery.

chain.cause: When the ventricle relaxes and blood starts to slip back toward it, blood fills the semilunar cusps' pockets.
chain.effect: The three pockets bulge together and seal, so blood does not flow back into the ventricle.

misconception.wrong: The left ventricle has a thicker wall because it pumps more blood than the right ventricle.
misconception.right: On average, both ventricles pump the same volume of blood each beat. The left wall is thicker because the vessels of the whole body resist flow far more than the vessels of the lungs, so the left ventricle has to generate about five times the pressure (about 120 versus 25 mm Hg). Heart muscle thickens when it works against a heavier load.

summary: Two atria receive blood from veins; two ventricles pump it into arteries. The venae cavae enter the right atrium, the pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle, the pulmonary veins enter the left atrium, and the aorta leaves the left ventricle. The tricuspid and mitral valves sit between atria and ventricles and are held by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles; the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves guard the exits and close by filling like pockets. Three septa divide the chambers, and the fossa ovalis marks the interatrial septum. The left ventricle wall is thickest because it works against the highest pressure. The cardiac skeleton anchors the valves and muscle and stops electrical signals crossing straight from atria to ventricles.
